title: Six Flags temporarily closes 9 roller-coasters, including 3 in Canada, after Georgia fatality

image.caption: A roller-coaster is shown at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. One man died and several others were injured in an incident involving a roller-coaster at the park. (Emilie Megnien/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated
Police are investigating after a man fell to his death from a roller coaster at a Six Flags near Atlanta, watched by other visitors to the amusement park as he was catapulted from the ride.
Officials haven't yet given details about what happened on Six Flags Over Georgia ride
Police are investigating after a man fell to his death from a roller-coaster at a Six Flags near Atlanta, watched by other visitors to the amusement park as he was catapulted from the ride.

Officials have not confirmed how the man died Monday at Six Flags Over Georgia in Austell, Ga., about 24 kilometres northwest of Atlanta. No information has been released about the condition of several others who were hurt.
Cobb County Police Department major crimes unit detectives are investigating.

Attractions at the parks that are similar to the coaster in Austell were closed "out of an abundance of caution," according to a Six Flags Entertainment Corporation spokesperson, who said staff members and local authorities responded immediately and the park is co-operating with the investigation.
"We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today," the spokesperson said, adding that the company is providing support to guests and staff who were impacted.

CBC News has confirmed that the list of nine rides includes the Behemoth and Leviathan at Canada's Wonderland, located north of Toronto. A park spokesperson said it did not have a timeline for when the rides might be available again.
One dead, several injured after incident on a Six Flags roller-coaster in Georgia | Hanomansing Live
Canada's Wonderland is open to the public for 12 more Halloween-themed evenings and weekends until it closes for the winter.

Montreal's La Ronde amusement park said it was temporarily shutting down its Goliath roller-coaster until an update is received from the manufacturer of the ride. La Ronde was a Six Flags property until this spring, when the park's purchase by EPR Properties was finalized.
Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the roller-coaster at the Georgia location. However, local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster.
Logan Conner said he was on the Goliath with his fiancée when he saw the man come out of his seat.
"The man started levitating in the air sideways," he told NBC. "We made direct eye contact with him."

blocks.text: Britny Landry had been on the ride earlier Monday and was waiting in line to go again. She could see part of the Goliath track.
"We just look, and I just see somebody fly out," she told KTVU-TV. She said she wasn't sure if that's what she saw at first. "Maybe somebody had a bag or something."

The roller-coaster, which was opened in 2006, reaches top speeds of about 113 km/h and heights of 61 metres, the park's website reports. During about 3½ minutes, riders "navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills," according to the website.

"I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one," Lisa Cupid, chair of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners, said in a statement. She added that next of kin have been notified.
The amusement park is a major part of the county's tourism and brings in visitors from across the southeast, Cupid said.
"We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories," she said.

This death would be at least the seventh at the Georgia park, including one in 2006 in which a man had a likely heart attack on the Goliath coaster, according to the Doan Law Firm, which focuses on amusement park accidents.

It also comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain, in Southern California, announced that it is retiring its famous X2 roller-coaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. The park had settled one wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022.

Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed roller-coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries, and his death was ruled accidental.
With files from CBC News
